newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong fire rules in question after deadly blaze.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong fire rules in question after deadly blaze.

text.p: Fire regulations and the safety of older buildings were in question in Hong Kong on Thursday after a blaze tore through a commercial highrise, leaving at least 39 people dead.

"We want particularly to know what lessons can be learnt from this, if the law is inadequate, what can be done," Chief Secretary Anson Chan told reporters after visiting some of the injured in hospital.
"We know particularly that this building was a pre-1973 building that is not caught by existing legislation," she said.

The fire, believed by some to have been sparked by an electrical fault in a lift, quickly engulfed the bottom four floors of the 16-storey Garley Building and shot through the elevator shaft to flats and offices on the upper floors, trapping many of the victims.
C.S. Chan of the fire department's Fire Protection Bureau said buildings are subject to the fire safety requirements in force when they were first occupied.
"For those old buildings, for example the Garley Building, you have no sprinklers by the time it was built, so it has no contravention to our existing regulations," he said.
"Before, those fire service installation requirements were not as stringent as nowdays," he said.
The building on Nathan Road, the main artery in the bustling Kowloon district, also had no fire alarms.
Firefighters said they were hampered by locked doors and a lack of extinguishers and other fire-fighting equipment.
Every day, many thousands of residents and tourists teem along Nathan Road and through the nearby warrens of camera shops, jewellery stores, clothing boutiques and restaurants.
The area is also a cluster of office blocks, workshops and commercial buildings.

Chan said the Fire Protection Bureau had been advising owners of older commercial and industrial buildings to "enhance the fire service installations in the interest of public safety" but added that they were under no obligation to comply.
"Currently there is no legislation to force them to follow the current standards or to bring them up to the current standards," he said.
A new fire safety bill was put before the Legislative Council on May 29 but has yet to be passed.

Chan said new buildings are subject to consultation with the bureau, which devises anti-fire requirements based on the plans, inspects the site after construction and then issues a fire services certificate.
All buildings must be inspected and maintained by a registered fire services contractor once a year, he said.
The date of the last inspection at the Garley Building was among the details investigators would be looking at, he said.

Caesar Lau, director of Webster Engineers Ltd, one of several hundred fire protection companies in the territory, said it was architecturally difficult for many older buildings to be upgraded with sprinklers, smoke detectors and hosereel systems.
Sprinklers are the most effective system, Lau said, although older buildings could be made safer by installing smoke detectors and opening sealed windows.

"The easiest way is to install the smoke detection system -- this system can give a very early alarm," Lau said. "The second is to provide more openable windows ... If the smoke is vented, most of the people can escape the fire."
